articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2M tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: The Tourist Development Council quietly extended its marketing agreement with a Tallahassee firm last week. Three board members have ties to the company.
brief: Escambia County's Tourist Development Council approved a $4.2 million contract extension with Sunshine State Marketing Group without soliciting competitive bids
Three of the nine TDC board members have financial or professional connections to the Tallahassee-based firm
Florida's public procurement laws allow but do not require competitive bidding for professional services contracts
articles.body:
The conference room on the third floor of the Escambia County governmental complex was half-empty last Tuesday afternoon. Seven of the nine Tourist Development Council members sat around the horseshoe table. The agenda item took four minutes.

No public comment. No discussion. A unanimous vote to extend a $4.2 million marketing contract with Sunshine State Marketing Group through 2029.

The Tallahassee-based firm has held Escambia County's destination marketing contract since 2019. This renewal marks the third consecutive extension awarded without a competitive bidding process.

The contract

Under Florida law, counties are not required to competitively bid professional services contracts. The state treats marketing and advertising as professional services, leaving procurement decisions to local discretion.

Escambia County's own purchasing policy encourages but does not mandate competitive solicitation for contracts exceeding $1 million.

"The board has the authority to extend existing agreements when the vendor has performed satisfactorily," said TDC Executive Director Marcus Webb in an email response to questions from The Flightline. "Sunshine State Marketing Group has consistently delivered results for our tourism economy."

Webb declined a request for an in-person interview.

The new contract increases annual compensation from $1.2 million to $1.4 million and adds performance bonuses tied to hotel occupancy rates and visitor spending metrics. The Flightline obtained the contract through a public records request.

Board connections

Three TDC board members have ties to Sunshine State Marketing Group that were not disclosed during last week's meeting.

Board member Patricia Harmon owns a 12% stake in Gulf Coast Hospitality Ventures, a hotel management company that has separately contracted with Sunshine State Marketing Group for property-specific advertising. State corporate filings confirm Harmon's ownership stake. She did not respond to phone and email requests for comment.

Board member David Chen's wife, Linda Chen, worked as a regional account director for Sunshine State Marketing Group from 2021 to 2024, according to her LinkedIn profile. Chen voted to approve the contract extension. Reached by phone, he said his wife's former employment was "not relevant" and declined further comment.

Board member Robert Fitzgerald serves on the advisory board of Visit Florida, the state tourism agency. Sunshine State Marketing Group holds three active contracts with Visit Florida totaling $8.7 million, according to the state's transparency portal. Fitzgerald did not respond to requests for comment.

Florida law requires public officials to disclose conflicts of interest before voting. None of the three board members filed conflict disclosures with the county clerk's office related to this contract, according to records reviewed by The Flightline.

The firm

Sunshine State Marketing Group was founded in 2012 by former Florida Division of Tourism employees. The company now holds destination marketing contracts with fourteen Florida counties, according to its website.

The firm's founder and CEO, Thomas Rayburn, has donated $47,500 to Florida political campaigns since 2018, state campaign finance records show. Recipients include three current Escambia County commissioners and the campaign committee of a former TDC board chair.

Rayburn did not respond to emailed questions about the company's relationship with TDC board members or its procurement practices.

Tourism tax dollars

The TDC contract is funded entirely by the county's tourist development tax—a 5% levy on short-term lodging that generated $18.3 million in fiscal year 2025, according to county budget documents.

The tax cannot legally be spent on general government operations. State law restricts its use to tourism promotion, beach renourishment, and sports facilities.

Escambia County allocated $6.1 million of those funds to destination marketing in the current fiscal year. The Sunshine State Marketing Group contract represents roughly 69% of that budget line.

The remaining marketing dollars fund smaller contracts with local vendors for event sponsorships, social media content, and visitor center operations.

What the law allows

University of Florida public administration professor Sandra Mitchell said Florida's professional services exemption creates "a gray area that local governments navigate differently."

"The law gives wide latitude," Mitchell said in a phone interview. "Some counties compete everything over a certain threshold. Others rely on relationship continuity. Neither approach is illegal."

She noted that conflict-of-interest questions hinge on whether board members' connections are "direct enough to constitute a prohibited conflict under Florida Statutes Chapter 112."

"Owning stock in a company that also contracts with the vendor is probably not a legal conflict," Mitchell said. "But whether it passes the smell test is a different question."

No oversight request—yet

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who appoints two members to the TDC board, said he was unaware of the board members' connections to the contractor until contacted by The Flightline.

"I'd want to look into that," Bergosh said. "If there are issues with how this was handled, we should know about it."

He stopped short of calling for an investigation or audit.

"The TDC operates with a lot of independence," Bergosh said. "That's by design. But independence doesn't mean no accountability."

The county commission has the authority to request audits of TDC spending through the clerk of court's office. No such request has been filed related to the marketing contract.

The next TDC meeting is scheduled for June 18. The agenda has not been published.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's empty storefronts: A block-by-block count
articles.dek: Palafox Street looks busy on weekend nights. But walk the side streets on a Tuesday morning and the vacancy pattern tells a different story about the post-pandemic recovery.
brief: A Flightline survey counted 47 vacant storefronts in downtown Pensacola's commercial core, representing roughly 18% of ground-floor retail space
Vacancy clusters on east-west streets like Intendencia and Main while Palafox maintains less than 10% vacancy
Property owners cite rising insurance costs and tenant demands for build-out allowances as barriers to filling empty spaces
articles.body:
The window at 27 East Intendencia Street still advertises a jewelry store that closed in 2023. Next door, brown paper covers the glass where a coffee shop operated for eight months before the owner moved to Gulf Breeze. Across the street, a faded "For Lease" sign lists a phone number that rings to voicemail.

This is downtown Pensacola at 10 a.m. on a Tuesday. Three blocks south, Palafox Street hums with the morning rush at coffee shops and breakfast spots. But the side streets tell a different story—one that six years of post-pandemic recovery hasn't fully rewritten.

The Flightline spent two weeks in May walking every block of downtown's commercial core, from Main Street north to Wright Street, Baylen to Alcaniz. We photographed storefronts, checked lease listings, and talked to property owners and business operators. The count: 47 vacant ground-floor commercial spaces in an area with roughly 260 such units.

That's an 18% vacancy rate. Not catastrophic. But not healthy either.

The geography of empty

Vacancy doesn't distribute evenly. Palafox Street between Garden and Main—the stretch tourists photograph, where Gallery Night draws thousands—shows only six empty storefronts. That's less than 10% of available space on the city's showcase corridor.

Walk one block east to Jefferson Street and the picture changes. Eleven vacancies. Two blocks west to Baylen, eight more. The east-west connectors fare worst: Intendencia Street between Palafox and Tarragona has five consecutive empty storefronts on its south side.

"Palafox is the runway," said Marcus Chen, who owns a men's clothing store on South Palafox. "Everything else is backstage. Landlords on the side streets want Palafox rents without Palafox foot traffic."

Chen pays $32 per square foot annually for his 1,200-square-foot space. Comparable storefronts on Jefferson list at $24 to $28 per square foot—lower, but not proportionally lower given the traffic difference.

The insurance factor

Rent isn't the only barrier. Every property owner we interviewed mentioned insurance.

Commercial property insurance rates in Escambia County have risen 40% to 60% since 2022, according to data from the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. For older downtown buildings—many constructed before 1950—the increases hit harder. Insurers charge premiums for aging electrical systems, flat roofs, and proximity to the waterfront.

"I'm paying $47,000 a year to insure a building I bought for $380,000 in 2019," said Patricia Womack, who owns three commercial properties on East Government Street. Two of her ground-floor units sit empty. "I can't drop rents low enough to attract tenants without losing money on the insurance alone."

Womack said she's had interest from prospective tenants but can't agree on terms. Specifically, she can't offer the build-out allowances that new businesses increasingly expect.

"Five years ago, tenants signed leases and did their own improvements," she said. "Now everyone wants $50,000 in tenant improvements before they'll commit. I don't have that sitting around for a space that rents for $2,000 a month."

What fills the gaps

Not every vacancy stays empty forever. The Flightline identified 12 storefronts that have turned over at least twice since 2022. The pattern: short-term leases, concept changes, closures.

The space at 120 South Palafox has housed a dessert bar, a vintage clothing pop-up, and briefly a CBD retailer. It's now listed again at $38 per square foot. The building's owner, a Tallahassee-based LLC, did not respond to requests for comment.

Some property owners have stopped trying for traditional retail tenants altogether. Three downtown storefronts now operate as short-term event spaces, rentable by the hour for private parties or photo shoots. Two others have converted to office use, their windows frosted for privacy.

"The retail-first mentality is a relic," said David Baxter, a commercial real estate broker with Pensacola-based NAI Pensacola. "Smart landlords are looking at flex space, service businesses, anything that doesn't depend on walk-in traffic."

Baxter pointed to the 200 block of East Main Street, where a former antique mall now houses a physical therapy clinic, a CPA office, and a podcast recording studio. "That building sat half-empty for two years trying to find retail tenants. Now it's 100% occupied with five-year leases."

The city's view

Downtown Pensacola falls under the jurisdiction of the Community Redevelopment Agency, which operates with a board identical to the Pensacola City Council. The CRA collects tax increment financing from the district—property tax revenue above a frozen baseline—and reinvests it in the area.

CRA director Amanda Rhodes said the agency tracks vacancy but doesn't publish regular reports. She estimated the rate at "somewhere in the mid-teens, percentage-wise," before we shared our count.

"Eighteen percent wouldn't surprise me," Rhodes said. "We're in a transition period. The businesses that thrived on pandemic-era spending patterns—home goods, specialty food—are consolidating. What comes next isn't clear yet."

The CRA's current strategic plan, adopted in 2024, emphasizes residential density over retail recruitment. The theory: more people living downtown creates organic demand for services and shops. Since 2020, roughly 400 new residential units have come online in the CRA district, with another 280 under construction.

"You can't program retail from the top down," Rhodes said. "You create conditions. Density is the condition."

What the numbers miss

A vacancy count captures a moment. It doesn't capture trajectory.

Five of the 47 empty storefronts we documented have active building permits for renovation. At least three have signed leases with tenants preparing to open this summer, according to lease listings and property owner interviews. The former Pensacola News Journal building on Romana Street, empty since 2021, is under contract for conversion to a boutique hotel with ground-floor restaurant space.

But new vacancies keep appearing. Since we began our count in early May, two more businesses have announced closures: a kitchen supply store on West Government Street and a women's boutique on Jefferson that had operated for 11 years.

The boutique's owner, Sandra Mitchell, said she'd tried to negotiate a rent reduction with her landlord. "They came down 5%. I needed 20% to make the numbers work."

Mitchell plans to continue selling online. Her storefront will add to the count.

Reading the windows

Empty storefronts communicate. Brown paper says "we're working on something." Bare windows with a "For Lease" sign say "waiting." Soap-scrawled messages advertising the previous tenant's new location say "we didn't fail, we moved." Windows dark and unsigned say nothing at all, which might be the most honest message.

Downtown Pensacola has all of these. The mix suggests neither collapse nor boom—just the slow, uneven metabolism of a small city's commercial core trying to find its equilibrium.

Walk Palafox on a Saturday night and the vacancy rate is invisible. Walk Intendencia on a Tuesday morning and it's the only thing you see.

Both walks tell the truth. Neither tells the whole story.

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors and a stressed-out city
articles.dek: Memorial Day weekend means the team's return to Pensacola Beach. It also means gridlocked traffic on Via de Luna, overflowing trash cans, and a test of whether the city's infrastructure can handle the crowds.
brief: An estimated 200,000 spectators descended on Pensacola Beach for the Blue Angels homecoming show, the largest crowd since 2019.
Traffic on the Bob Sikes Bridge backed up for three hours Saturday afternoon, with some visitors reporting 90-minute waits to cross.
Santa Rosa County officials are calling for a post-event review of crowd management protocols after trash collection and emergency response systems were overwhelmed.
articles.body:
The first F/A-18 Super Hornet screamed over Casino Beach at 2:47 p.m. Saturday, trailing white smoke against a cloudless sky. On the sand below, 85,000 people craned their necks upward. Another 40,000 watched from boats anchored in the Santa Rosa Sound. Thousands more lined Via de Luna Drive, perched on coolers and tailgates, phones raised to capture the moment.

This is what homecoming looks like for the Blue Angels. It is also what 200,000 people trying to occupy a barrier island built for a fraction of that number looks like.

By 4 p.m., the Bob Sikes Bridge had become a parking lot. The backup stretched past Tiger Point. Drivers who had planned a quick beach trip found themselves trapped in a three-hour crawl. Some turned off their engines and waited. Others abandoned the attempt entirely, making U-turns on Highway 98 and heading home.

"We left Gulf Breeze at 1:30 thinking we'd have plenty of time," said Marcus Henderson, a Navarre resident who brought his two sons to see their first air show. "We didn't get across the bridge until almost 5. The show was basically over."

The math doesn't work

Pensacola Beach has one road in and one road out. The Bob Sikes Bridge, a two-lane span connecting Gulf Breeze to the island, handles roughly 15,000 vehicles on a typical summer Saturday. During Blue Angels weekend, that number can triple.

Santa Rosa County Sheriff Bob Johnson acknowledged the bottleneck during a press briefing Sunday morning.

"We had every deputy we could spare directing traffic," Johnson said. "But there's only so much you can do when you've got that volume trying to move through a single chokepoint."

The Escambia County Sheriff's Office, which handles beach patrol, reported no major incidents during the show itself. But the hours after the final flyover tested the system. Deputies responded to seven fender-benders on Via de Luna, all attributed to stop-and-go congestion. Two heat-related medical calls came in from spectators stuck in traffic without air conditioning.

Pensacola Beach's volunteer fire department handled both calls. Chief Tom Browning said his crews were stretched thin.

"We've got 22 volunteers," Browning said. "On a weekend like this, we need twice that."

Trash, traffic and the tourism trade-off

By Sunday morning, the evidence of Saturday's crowds was everywhere. Overflowing trash cans lined the boardwalk. Plastic cups and aluminum cans dotted the dunes. A cleanup crew from Keep Pensacola Beautiful collected 2.3 tons of debris from the beach and parking areas—a single-day record for the organization.

"People come here to enjoy the beach, and I get that," said Angela Morrison, who coordinates the nonprofit's volunteer efforts. "But the infrastructure just isn't designed for this. We had cans that were full by noon. There was nowhere for people to put their trash."

Santa Rosa County Commissioner Kerry Smith toured the beach Sunday afternoon. He called the scene "predictable" and said county officials would conduct a formal review of crowd management protocols before next year's show.

"We love the Blue Angels. They're part of who we are," Smith said. "But we owe it to our residents and our visitors to do this better."

Smith declined to specify what changes might be considered. Options discussed in previous years have included mandatory shuttle service from remote parking lots, timed entry permits for the beach and staggered show times to spread out vehicle traffic. None have been implemented.

The economic argument

For all the headaches, the Blue Angels homecoming remains one of the region's largest economic drivers. Visit Pensacola, the area's tourism marketing organization, estimates the weekend generates between $25 million and $30 million in direct spending—hotel rooms, restaurant meals, gas and souvenirs.

Davin Ruohomaki, the organization's president, pushed back against criticism of the event's management.

"Is there traffic? Yes. Is it crowded? Absolutely," Ruohomaki said. "But this is a signature event for our community. People plan their vacations around it. They come from all over the country."

Hotel occupancy in Pensacola Beach hit 98 percent Friday and Saturday nights, according to data from the Santa Rosa Island Authority. Rates at beachfront properties averaged $389 per night, up from $245 on a typical Memorial Day weekend.

Margaritaville Beach Hotel general manager Stephanie Byrd said her property sold out six weeks in advance.

"Our guests understand what they're signing up for," Byrd said. "They know it's going to be packed. They plan accordingly. And honestly, most of them love the energy."

A question of capacity

The tension between economic benefit and livability is not new to Pensacola Beach. The island has wrestled with growth pressures for decades, caught between its identity as a laid-back beach community and its role as Escambia County's tourism engine.

The Blue Angels homecoming sharpens that tension into a single weekend.

"Every year we have this conversation," said Dave Pavlock, a longtime beach resident who serves on the Santa Rosa Island Authority's advisory committee. "How many people is too many? At what point does the experience become so degraded that people stop coming?"

Pavlock doesn't claim to have the answer. But he thinks the question deserves more serious consideration than it typically receives.

"The default assumption is always: more visitors, more money, that's good," he said. "But there are costs. Real costs. To our roads, our environment, our quality of life. At some point, the county has to decide what kind of place this is going to be."

For now, the jets have returned to their hangar at NAS Pensacola. The crowds have dispersed. The trash has been collected, mostly. The bridge is flowing freely again.

Until next year.
